lesson.title: The Long Run Average: Understanding Expected Value
lesson.summary: The expected value of a discrete random variable is the probability weighted average of its possible outcomes, the long run average value you would see if the chance process repeated many, many times.
lesson.body:
In an ordinary data set, you find the mean by adding up all the values and dividing by how many there are. Expected value applies that same averaging idea to a random variable before you ever collect data, using the probabilities from its distribution as weights instead of counting actual observations. Expected value is written E(X), or sometimes with the Greek letter mu with a subscript X, and it plays the same role for a random variable that the mean plays for a data set.

The formula is E(X) equals the sum, over every possible value x, of x times P(X = x). In words, multiply each possible outcome by its own probability, then add up all those products. Outcomes that are more likely pull the average toward them more strongly, the same way a value that appears more often in a data set pulls an ordinary mean toward it. A value with a tiny probability barely nudges the expected value at all, even if that value itself is large.

Return once more to X, the number of pets owned by a randomly selected student, with the valid distribution x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and probabilities 0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1 confirmed in the previous chapter. Applying the formula:

E(X) = 0(0.2) + 1(0.4) + 2(0.3) + 3(0.1)
E(X) = 0 + 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.3
E(X) = 1.3

So the expected number of pets is 1.3.

It is worth pausing on what this number does and does not mean. No individual student owns 1.3 pets, that is not even one of the four possible values, and you cannot own a fraction of a pet. E(X) = 1.3 is instead the balance point of the entire distribution, the value the average would settle near if you sampled an enormous number of students and averaged their pet counts. This connects to the idea behind the law of large numbers: the more times a chance process is repeated, the closer the average of the results tends to get to the expected value.

Knowing E(X) = 1.3 tells you where the distribution is centered, but it says nothing about how spread out the values are around that center. Two very different populations of students, one where almost everyone owns exactly 1 pet and one where pet ownership varies wildly from 0 to 3, could both have the same expected value. Measuring that spread is the job of variance, which the next two chapters build directly on top of expected value.
